passage:
I'm Divyansh, and last year I thought "lazy" was just my name. Every evening I sat with my maths book and looked out of the window, and Mummy said, "Lazy boy, again?" Papa said it too. After a while I said it myself: "I can't, I'm lazy." It felt true, like being short.
Then Mohit Mama came to stay for the holidays. He didn't scold. He sat on the bed next to me with his newspaper and said, "Just the first two sums. I'll be right here." He wrote the steps on a slip: read, underline the numbers, do sum one.
I did sum one. Then two. Then the rest.
I'm still slow sometimes. But now I know I'm not lazy. I just get stuck at the start.

qa.q: What steps did Mohit Mama write on the slip?
qa.a: Read, underline the numbers, do sum one.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh start saying 'I can't, I'm lazy'?
qa.a: He felt discouraged by hearing 'lazy' from Mummy and Papa every evening, until he believed it was a fact about himself, like being short.

qa.q: What worked better than scolding for Divyansh?
qa.a: Breaking the homework into small written steps and having Mohit Mama sit nearby for the start helped him begin and finish.

qa.q: How might Mummy and Papa see Divyansh's homework differently if they tried Mohit Mama's way?
qa.a: They might see that he isn't lazy but gets stuck at the start, and that sitting nearby helps more than calling him names.

grounding: Shows a child who took on the label 'lazy' from his parents, and how small steps with an adult sitting nearby helped more than scolding.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Saurabh Mehra, Friday
During homework hour, Chetan sat with his English worksheet for twenty minutes without writing a word. When I came over, he said quietly, "I'm lazy, sir. Papa says I'm the laziest in the house." He said it flatly, like reading out his roll number. His shoulders were up near his ears.
I don't think he is lazy. He seemed stuck, and ashamed.
What I did next: I pulled a chair beside him and folded the worksheet so only question 1 showed. "Just this one. I'll sit here." He finished it in three minutes, then unfolded the next part himself.
At pickup I spoke with his father privately, shared what had helped, and suggested sitting near Chetan for the first few minutes at home instead of scolding. He listened and said he would try.

qa.q: How long did Chetan sit with the worksheet without writing?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Chetan's flat 'I'm lazy, sir' suggest about how he sees himself?
qa.a: He has come to believe being lazy is simply a fact about him, and his raised shoulders suggest shame.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Chetan start?
qa.a: He sat beside Chetan and folded the worksheet so only question 1 showed, making the first step small.

qa.q: How might Chetan's father feel hearing the teacher's suggestion at pickup?
qa.a: He may feel a little surprised or embarrassed, but hearing privately what worked seems to make him open to sitting nearby instead of scolding.

grounding: Illustrates a child who repeats his father's 'lazy' label as fact, and a teacher who helps by shrinking the task and sitting nearby.

passage:
Lavanya, beta, your father called you lazy today? Come, sit. Let me tell you about when I was nine.
Every evening I dawdled over homework. My father would say, "Anirban, you're lazy. You'll never do anything." After a while I believed him. Why try, if I was just lazy?
Then my uncle came to stay. One evening he pulled a chair beside me and said, "What's the first small thing?" I said, "Copy the question." "Do that. I'll sit here." So I did. Then, "What's next?"
He never called me lazy. He just broke it into little steps and sat with me at the start. I finished that homework, beta. And I stopped believing I was lazy.

qa.q: How old was Anirban when he dawdled over homework?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What was young Anirban feeling after being called lazy again and again?
qa.a: Young Anirban felt ashamed and hopeless, starting to believe the word lazy, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: In the story, what did the uncle do that helped?
qa.a: He broke the homework into small steps and sat beside Anirban at the start, without calling him lazy.

qa.q: How might Anirban's father have felt seeing the homework finished?
qa.a: He may have been surprised, perhaps realising that calling Anirban lazy hadn't helped.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling being called lazy as a child until it felt true, and an uncle who helped by breaking tasks into steps.

passage:
The power had gone, the exam was tomorrow, and Deepika had been staring at her geography book by candlelight for an hour. Her father Nitin, back late from work, snapped. "Still on page one? You're so lazy, Deepika!"
Deepika's face went hot. She thought: he's right. I am lazy. I'm always like this.
She put her head down on the book.
Nitin stood there. Then he sighed, pulled a stool next to her and sat. "Sorry. That wasn't fair. Let's do just the first question together. Read it to me."
Deepika sniffed and read it. Then they did the second. By the time the power came back, she was on page four.

qa.q: What subject was Deepika studying?
qa.a: Geography.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when her father called her lazy?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hurt, starting to believe it was simply true about her.

qa.q: What helped more than scolding, and why?
qa.a: Nitin apologising, sitting beside her and starting with just one question, which made the task feel manageable.

qa.q: What might Nitin be feeling when he pulls up the stool?
qa.a: Nitin probably feels tired and regretful, realising his words hurt more than helped.

grounding: Shows a child called lazy by her father while dawdling over homework, starting to believe it, until he sits beside her and breaks it into steps.

passage:
Every evening in their Aizawl flat, Lalremsiami took ages over homework. She'd sharpen pencils, stare, fidget. Her mother, Aparna, would say from the kitchen, "Why are you so lazy? Your cousin finishes in half an hour."
One evening Lalremsiami whispered to herself, "I'm the lazy one. That's just me."
Aparna heard it. She stopped chopping onions.
The next evening, she didn't say "lazy". She sat at the table with her tea and said, "What's the very first thing on your list?" "Maths question one." "Just that. I'll sit here."
Lalremsiami did question one. Then two. She looked up, surprised. Aparna smiled and kept drinking her tea.

qa.q: Who did Aparna say finishes in half an hour?
qa.a: Lalremsiami's cousin.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she whispered "That's just me"?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and sad, starting to believe she was simply lazy.

qa.q: What did Aparna change, and why did it help?
qa.a: She stopped calling her lazy, sat nearby and focused on the first small step, which made starting easier.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she stopped chopping onions?
qa.a: Aparna seemed shaken and regretful, realising her words had become Lalremsiami's belief about herself.

grounding: Shows a child called lazy for dawdling who starts to believe it, and a mother who switches to small steps and sitting nearby.

passage:
"Ojas, forty minutes and you've written two lines!" Kamal stood in the doorway. "Such a lazy boy."
Ojas kept his eyes on the notebook. "I'm lazy," he said flatly. "Everyone says."
"I didn't mean..." Kamal stopped. "Who's everyone?"
"You. Dadi. Ma'am wrote it in my diary." He pushed the notebook away. "Lazy people can't do essays."
Kamal pulled up a chair. "Okay. What's the essay?"
"My Favourite Festival. Two pages."
"Two pages is too big to look at. Let's do one piece. Which festival?"
"Onam."
"What's the first thing you see on Onam morning?"
"The pookalam. Amma's flowers."
"Write just that sentence. I'll sit here."
Ojas wrote it. Then another. "Papa, don't go."
"I'm right here."

qa.q: What is the title of Ojas's essay?
qa.a: My Favourite Festival.

qa.q: What does Ojas's "I'm lazy, everyone says" reveal about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels hurt and discouraged, and now believes being lazy is simply a fact about himself.

qa.q: What does Kamal switch to that works better than scolding?
qa.a: He sits nearby and breaks the essay into one small piece, the first thing Ojas sees on Onam morning.

qa.q: What might Kamal feel when Ojas repeats "I'm lazy"?
qa.a: Kamal seems shaken and regretful, stopping mid-sentence on hearing his own word coming back.

grounding: Shows a child who has been called lazy starting to believe it, and a parent helping more by breaking the task down and sitting nearby.
